title: Search and Inverted Indexes
summary: Build full-text search with an inverted index, analyzers, BM25 ranking and sharded Elasticsearch kept in sync with the database through CDC.
body:
Any product with a search box eventually asks a question a primary database answers badly: "find posts containing *distributed* and *cache*, best matches first, in under 200 ms, across a billion documents." In an interview this appears in feed, e-commerce, ticketing, chat-history and log-analytics designs. The expected answer is a dedicated search index fed from the source of truth, plus a clear story for relevance, sharding and how stale results can be.

## Why `LIKE '%term%'` does not scale

A B-tree index orders values by their prefix, so `WHERE title LIKE 'redis%'` can seek to a range. A leading wildcard (`LIKE '%redis%'`) has no prefix to seek on, so the database scans every row and runs a substring match. It also has no notion of words, stemming ("caching" vs "cache"), case folding, typo tolerance or relevance ranking. PostgreSQL can go further with `tsvector` full-text search and trigram (`pg_trgm`) GIN indexes, which is a reasonable answer at modest scale when you want one fewer system. Past tens of millions of documents, heavy query volume or rich ranking and faceting, teams move to a search engine such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Solr, all built on Apache Lucene.

## The inverted index

A book index maps words to page numbers. An inverted index does the same: for every **term** it stores a **postings list** of the document IDs that contain it, often with term frequency and positions. A query for two terms intersects two sorted postings lists instead of scanning documents.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    D1["Doc 1: Caching with Redis"] --> AN["Analyzer: tokenize, lowercase, stem"]
    D2["Doc 2: Redis cluster sharding"] --> AN
    AN --> T1["cach: 1"]
    AN --> T2["redis: 1, 2"]
    AN --> T3["cluster: 2"]
    AN --> T4["shard: 2"]
    Q["Query: redis caching"] --> QA["Same analyzer"]
    QA --> M["Intersect postings: doc 1"]
    T1 --> M
    T2 --> M
```

Both documents pass through an **analyzer**. A typical analyzer has a tokenizer (split on whitespace and punctuation), token filters (lowercase, remove stop words like "with", stem "caching" to "cach") and optionally synonyms. The query text must go through the same analyzer, otherwise "Caching" would never match the stored term "cach". Intersecting the postings for "redis" (1, 2) and "cach" (1) returns document 1. Analyzer choice is a product decision: stemming improves recall for prose but is wrong for product SKUs, email addresses and code identifiers, which want keyword (exact) fields.

Lucene writes the index as immutable **segments**. New documents go to an in-memory buffer; a **refresh** turns the buffer into a new searchable segment, and background merges combine small segments and purge deleted documents. Updates are delete-plus-reinsert. This is why search engines are **near-real-time**: in Elasticsearch a document becomes searchable after the next refresh (default interval 1 second), not at write time. Calling refresh on every write destroys indexing throughput.

## Ranking in brief

Matching produces candidates; ranking orders them. The default scorer in Lucene-based engines is **BM25**. A term contributes more when it is frequent in the document, with diminishing returns (controlled by `k1`, default 1.2), when it is rare across the corpus (inverse document frequency), and when the document is short relative to average (length normalization, `b`, default 0.75). Real products then combine text score with business signals such as recency, popularity, personalization or a learned ranking model, often as a second-stage re-rank over the top few hundred candidates. In an interview, naming BM25 plus "boost by recency and engagement" is enough unless ranking is the focus.

## Shards, replicas and the query path

An index is split into **primary shards**, each a self-contained Lucene index holding a subset of documents (routed by hashing the document ID by default). Each primary has **replica shards** on other nodes for fault tolerance and read throughput. The primary shard count is fixed at index creation; changing it means reindexing (or the split/shrink APIs with constraints), so size shards up front. A common guideline is to keep shards in the low tens of gigabytes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant CO as Coordinating node
    participant S0 as Shard 0
    participant S1 as Shard 1
    participant S2 as Shard 2
    C->>CO: search "redis caching", top 10
    par query phase
        CO->>S0: top 10 IDs and scores
        CO->>S1: top 10 IDs and scores
        CO->>S2: top 10 IDs and scores
    end
    S0-->>CO: local top 10
    S1-->>CO: local top 10
    S2-->>CO: local top 10
    CO->>CO: merge to global top 10
    CO->>S1: fetch phase: full docs
    CO-->>C: 10 results
```

Because documents are spread by ID, every search fans out to one copy of every shard, each returns its local top 10, and the coordinating node merges them before fetching the winning documents. Latency is set by the slowest shard, and deep pagination is expensive: page 1,000 at 10 results per page asks every shard for its top 10,000 (Elasticsearch rejects offsets past 10,000 by default). Use `search_after` cursors instead of large offsets. If queries always filter by tenant, custom routing by tenant ID sends a query to one shard instead of all of them, at the risk of hot shards for large tenants.

## Keeping the index in sync

The search index is a **derived view**, not the source of truth. Writing to the database and then to Elasticsearch from application code is a dual write: if the second call fails or the process crashes, they diverge silently.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    APP["App service"] --> DB[("Postgres: source of truth")]
    DB -->|"WAL"| CDC["CDC connector (Debezium)"]
    CDC --> K[["Kafka topic keyed by doc id"]]
    K --> IDX["Indexer workers"]
    IDX --> ES[("Search cluster")]
    API["Search API"] --> ES
    API -->|"hydrate or verify"| DB
```

Change data capture reads committed changes from the database's replication log and publishes them, keyed by document ID so updates to one document stay ordered. Indexer workers batch them into bulk requests. Make the indexer idempotent and order-safe: use the database row version as an external version so a delayed older update cannot overwrite a newer one. Keep enough log retention to rebuild, and support a full reindex into a new index followed by an alias swap for mapping changes. Expect seconds of lag end to end, and design the product around it: after a user edits a listing, show the edited version from the database on their own page rather than relying on search. For permission-sensitive results, either index access control fields and filter on them, or re-check the top results against the database.

## Prefix search and autocomplete

Autocomplete has a tighter budget (often under 50 ms per keystroke) and matches prefixes, not whole words.

| Approach | How it works | Strength | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Trie with cached top-k per node | Walk prefix characters; each node stores the best k completions | Very fast, predictable | Memory heavy; offline rebuild for popularity changes |
| Edge n-grams at index time | "redis" indexed as r, re, red, redi, redis | Uses normal search engine and filters | Larger index; tune min and max gram |
| Completion suggester (FST) | Compressed finite-state structure in memory | Fast prefix lookups in Elasticsearch | Prefix only; limited filtering |
| B-tree prefix `LIKE 'red%'` | Range scan on ordered index | No new system | No ranking or typo tolerance |
| Full engine with BM25 | Inverted index over whole words | Relevance, filters, facets | Heavier per query |

Typo tolerance is usually fuzzy matching by edit distance (Lucene supports up to 2 edits), which multiplies query cost, so apply it only after a prefix match fails or on longer inputs.

## Failure modes and interview mistakes

- Treating the search cluster as a primary database. It can lose recent writes on failure and is rebuilt from the source.
- Forgetting the refresh delay, then promising read-your-writes through search.
- Too many tiny shards (overhead per shard) or too few huge ones (slow recovery, no parallelism).
- Deep offset pagination and unbounded wildcard or regex queries that scan the term dictionary.
- Dual writes from the application with no reconciliation.

## How to use it in an interview

Say: "Postgres is the source of truth; we stream changes through CDC and Kafka into Elasticsearch, so search is a few seconds stale, which is acceptable for discovery." Then give the numbers that size the cluster: document count times average indexed size (for example 500 million posts at 2 KB is about 1 TB, which with one replica is 2 TB, so roughly 40 primary shards at 25 GB), query rate and the p99 target. Expect follow-ups on relevance ("how do you rank?"), freshness ("user posts and immediately searches"), reindexing after a mapping change, and hot tenants.

## Interview exercise

Design search for a marketplace with 200 million listings, 5,000 queries per second and filters for category, price and location. Sketch the indexing pipeline, pick a shard count with your assumptions, choose analyzers for title text and for SKU, and explain what a seller sees if they search for their listing one second after editing it.

## Further reading

- [Elasticsearch reference: near real-time search](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/near-real-time.html) explains segments and refresh.
- [Apache Lucene](https://lucene.apache.org/) is the library underneath Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Solr.
- [Debezium documentation](https://debezium.io/documentation/) describes log-based change data capture into Kafka.
keyTakeaways: A leading-wildcard LIKE scans every row; an inverted index maps analyzed terms to postings lists.
Index and query text must use the same analyzer, and analyzer choice is a product decision.
Search fans out to every shard and merges top results, so shard count and pagination style drive latency.
The index is a derived view fed by CDC with versioned, idempotent updates, and it is near-real-time, not read-your-writes.
Autocomplete uses prefix structures such as tries, edge n-grams or a completion suggester.
